claims.text: The proposed approach will reduce lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 25% relative to Debye- or DFT-based analytical estimates.
The proposed approach will explicitly separate lattice and electronic heat transport.
The approach will correctly capture a reduced lattice contribution below approximately 200 K.
Lattice conduction is dominant from 300 to 1200 K in oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr.
The target alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr can exist as a metastable single beta-BCC phase.
The relevant initial material is defect-free or near single-phase.
The relevant specimens have less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed methodology incorporates DFT-computed, chemical-disorder-dependent force constants into phonon-dispersion calculations.
Electronic heat transport will be modeled independently through a separate electron-scattering framework.
The approach is applicable from approximately 200 to 1200 K for samples with negligible defects or impurities.
Chemical disorder in HfNbTaTiZr produces significant variations in interatomic force constants.
Disorder-induced force-constant variations alter phonon dispersion and phonon-scattering rates, thereby mediating lattice thermal conductivity.
Sampling atomic-scale force-constant fluctuations will yield more accurate phonon spectra and anharmonic scattering rates.
Separating phonon and electron models prevents conflation of lattice and electronic contributions and isolates lattice heat transport.
Predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be within 25% of experimental measurements for high-purity HfNbTaTiZr.
Below approximately 200 K, heat conduction is lattice-dominated, with lattice and electronic contributions becoming comparable under other conditions.
Prior Debye- or DFT-based analytical approaches typically conflate lattice and electronic transport and neglect full atomic-scale disorder.
In oxygen-contaminated or heavily defected specimens, additional scattering phenomena not represented by the model would likely dominate.
Time-domain thermoreflectance or transient thermal-grating measurements can independently resolve lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity components over 150 to 1200 K.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that lattice conduction is dominant at high temperatures of 300–1200 K, whereas the predicted outcome describes conduction as lattice-dominated below approximately 200 K and subsequently comparable with electronic conduction.
The stated applicability begins at approximately 200 K, but the hypothesis makes a claim about behavior below 200 K and the falsification experiment tests down to 150 K.
